text:
Helper functions


Click here to view the helper functions of this document


save_figure()
save_figure() is specific for manuscript figures.

save_figure <- function(p, filename, width = 17, height = 20, unit = "cm") {
  ## Save image on disk as png and pdf
  file_png <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(filename, ".png"))
  ggsave(file_png, p, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150, units = unit)
  file_pdf <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(filename, ".pdf"))
  ggsave(file_pdf, p, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150, units = unit)

}



load_rds()
Loads the .rds files from disk

load_rds <- function(figure = NULL) {
  file_rds <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(figure, ".rds"))
  readRDS(file_rds)
}

title: 9. Junction differential expression; between astrocyte clusters
text:
In script 08 I created gene-specific junction Seurat objects of the astrocytes, with the dimensionality reductions and cluster annotation I made with the short-read data transferred to it. In this script I test which junctions of a gene are differentially expressed between the astrocyte clusters, using Seurat’s FindAllMarkers() (each cluster versus all other clusters). The next script (10) tests differential expression between ALS and controls with a pseudobulk approach.
For every gene, the full results are stored as a .csv, a dotplot of the top junctions is displayed, and a multi-page PDF with a UMAP feature plot and a violin plot for every junction is saved to disk for inspection.

This script was run with the conda environment r_scrnaseq_core.

Packages

# Basics
library(tidyverse)

library(knitr)
library(here)

# Analysis-specific
library(Seurat)
library(AnnotationHub) # To connect to ensembldb
library(ensembldb) # To get transcript information
# These Bioconductor packages (AnnotationHub and ensembldb) contain functions
# with the same name as several dplyr functions (select, filter, etc.), so I
# needed to specify those with dplyr:: thoroughout this script



Directories

# Get string of home directory. I used the here package, which sets the home
# directory when loading library(here)
dir_home <- here::here()

## Data directories
dir_raw <- file.path(dir_home, "data/raw")
dir_data <- file.path(dir_home, "data/processed")
dir_temp <- file.path(dir_home, "data/temporary")

## Results directories
# Create subfolders with the name of this script, so all figures/tables of
# this script are in the same place
folder_name <- knitr::current_input(dir = FALSE)
folder_name <- str_remove(folder_name, "\\.\\w*$")
dir_fig <- file.path(dir_home, "results/figures", folder_name)
dir.create(dir_fig, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir_tab <- file.path(dir_home, "results/tables", folder_name)
dir.create(dir_tab, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

## Manuscript figure directory 
# rds/grob objects for report figures land here, to be assembled by
# scripts/11_assemble_manuscript_figures.qmd
dir_man <- file.path(dir_home, "results/figures/manuscript")

## Cache directory
# For this script, I'm setting a cache directory; this is specific for the
# ensembldb loading for the exon junction plots. AnnotationHub downloads the 
# database to a cache folder. If I wouldn't manually set it, it would use the 
# cache of my home directory instead ("/path/to/folder"), which only 
# has 7 GB space
dir_cache <- file.path(dir_temp, "annotationhub_cache")
dir.create(dir_cache, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

text:
Non-canonical junctions of GFAP
I observed several significant non-canonical splicing events of GFAP. I wanted to display these on transcripts which matches them. I print the tibble with the results of which_known_transcript() - while you cannot see everything within it, you can see how many transcripts match it (and printing it with kable() became to broad a table to fit on the page, so I settled for the tibble).

Exon-skipping of exon 2 (chr17:44913824:44915025)

# Set default for all next GFAP visualizations
gene <- "GFAP"
exons_gene <- get_gene_exons(edb, gene)
# I looked up the xmin and xmax of the canonical transcript and will set this
# manually for all further GFAP transcripts
xmin <- 44902542
xmax <- 44916117

# Set junction
junction_to_plot <- "chr17:44913824:44915025"
# Extract junction label from the tibble in which I defined
junction_to_plot_label <- junctions_tibble[
  junctions_tibble$junction == junction_to_plot,
  "label"
  ]

# Examine which known junctions there are for this gene
tx_hits <- which_known_transcript(junction_to_plot, exons_gene, 
                                  type = "auto", tolerance = 0)

title: 7. Gene modules with hdWGCNA
text:
This script identifies co-expression modules in the astrocytes with hdWGCNA, the high-dimensional version of WGCNA for single-cell data. Because single-nuclei data is sparse, hdWGCNA first aggregates similar cells into metacells, then builds a co-expression network on them, and finally assigns genes to modules. The modules are examined (hub genes, module eigengenes on the UMAP).
Unfortunately, not too much time to investigate this. I planned on running GO-terms on it all, but did not manage to do so.

title: 5. Trajectory inference with Monocle3
text:
This script runs Monocle3, a trajectory inference tool that scores consistently high in benchmark papers, on the clustered astrocyte Seurat object. I use the clustered object because the untrustworthy clusters have already been removed there. The Seurat object is converted to a cell_data_set, a trajectory graph is learned on the astrocyte UMAP, and pseudotime is calculated from a chosen root.
I mainly ran monocle3 to test whether it constructs a similar trajectory as Slingshot; however, I found that monocle3 creates an incredibly detailed trajectory, but with only a single pseudotime scale, which makes it hard to do tests with it. I planned on running monocle3’s tests, such as graph_test() which tests whether a gene’s expression is spatially autocorrelated on the trajectory graph or find_gene_modules() which groups significant genes into modules of genes with similar behaviour along the trajectory, but unfortunately, due to the time constraints, I did not get to doing so .

Defining variables
This code block defines variables to be used throughout the rest of the document. If someone ever wants to run these scripts with different variables, they can easily change it here. I’ll substantiate any choices here

res
Slingshots requires you to run a clustering before you run Slingshot, as the trajectory inference depends on clustering. I will not add my annotated clusters from script 02_clustering.qmd; that just draws a trajectory across my clusters. I deliberately set a higher resolution. I tested it for multiple resolutions; none really made sense, 0.5 did the most, so I chose 0.5


reduction
Reduction sets the dimensionality reduction. I used ‘harmony’, the integrated PCA. In converting Seurat to a SingleCellExperiment object, dimensionality reductions get put into capslock; thus, I also entered it in capslock.


vars_ridges
I examined how pseudotime of lineages linked with metadata variables using ridgeplots; with pTDP-43 stage, primary site of onset, and disease subtypes, I can find direct links with ALS-pathology. I added gender as a sanity check and added anonymousID to see whether individual samples drive a certain signal.

Helper functions


Click here to view the helper functions of this document


theme_quarto() and theme_manuscript()
I created my own themes to add to figures. theme_quarto() is used to add themes to figures as displayed in the Quarto document and saved to disk as .pdf or .png. theme_manuscript() is used to add themes to figures as they will end up in the manuscript. I can already add arguments with theme() or specific themes (e.g. theme_classic(), my personal favourite) to plots; adding theme() afterwards keeps whatever was added in theme() before it, unless I specify that arugment here - that’s why I allowed to specify some things within my functions as well.

theme_quarto <- function(
    legend_position = "right", 
    plot_title = element_blank()
    ) {
    theme(
      plot.title = plot_title,
      legend.position = legend_position
    )
}

theme_manuscript <- function(
    legend_position = "none",
    plot_title = element_blank(),
    axis_title_size = 8,
    axis_text_size = 6
    ) {
    theme(
      plot.title = plot_title,
      legend.position = legend_position,
      axis.title = element_text(size = axis_title_size),
      axis.text = element_text(size = axis_text_size),
      legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"), 
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9)
    )
}



save_plot()
This document displays all the figures I make, but I also want them saved to disk — both as .png and .pdf. I only need to provide the ggplot object, a filename (without extension), and optionally the width and height of the figure and additional arguments put into themes.
The figures for my written report contain subfigures spread across multiple scripts. Since I want to assemble these panel figures via R code rather than by hand, save_plot() can also optionally save the plot object itself to disk as an .rds file, for a final script to later combine with patchwork. Set figure to the name the figure should carry in the report (e.g. "SF1A") to trigger this; leave it NULL (the default) to just save the .png/.pdf as normal.
A live ggplot object carries its underlying data along with it — for plots built from large Seurat objects, this can balloon the saved file to gigabytes. To avoid this, save_plot() converts the object to a grob (a static, pre-rendered drawing, with no data attached) before saving it as .rds. This is controlled by the grob argument, and defaults to TRUE, since converting a small plot costs nothing but forgetting to convert a large one is expensive. Set grob = FALSE only if a later step specifically needs the original, live ggplot object rather than its rendered form.

save_plot <- function(
    p, filename, 
    width = 10, height = 6, 
    figure = NULL, grob = TRUE, apply_theme = TRUE, 
    add_tag = TRUE, tag_text_size = 14,
    legend_pos_manuscript = "none"
    ) {
  ## Save image on disk as png and pdf
  # Add Quarto-specific theme, unless the plot has its own custom theme
  if (apply_theme) {
    p_image <- p + theme_quarto()
  } else {
    p_image <- p
  }
  file_png <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".png"))
  ggsave(file_png, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  file_pdf <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".pdf"))
  ggsave(file_pdf, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  
  ## Save the ggplot object on disk as an rds file 
  if (!is.null(figure)) {
    # Add tag if needed
    if (add_tag) {
      tag <- str_extract(figure, "[A-Z]$")
      p <- p + 
        labs(tag = tag) + 
        theme(
          plot.tag = element_text(
            face = "bold", 
            size = tag_text_size, 
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0
            )
        )
    }
    # Add manuscript-specific theme, unless the plot has its own custom theme
    if (apply_theme) {
      p <- p + theme_manuscript(legend_position = legend_pos_manuscript)
    }
    file_rds <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(figure, ".rds"))
    # Convert the object to a grob if needed
    if (grob) {
      p <- ggplotGrob(p)
    }
    # Save on disk
    saveRDS(p, file_rds)
  }
}



print_tabset()
Quarto cannot cross-reference figures that are made inside a loop. To still display the plots of a loop in this document, I collect them in a named list and show them as tabs with print_tabset(). The names of the list become the tab titles. It also accepts data frames (shown as a table). This function writes raw Quarto markdown, so the chunk that calls it needs the chunk option #| output: asis. heading_level should be one deeper than the heading above the chunk.

print_tabset <- function(obj_list, heading_level = 3) {
  cat("::: {.panel-tabset}\n\n")
  for (nm in names(obj_list)) {
    cat(strrep("#", heading_level), " ", nm, "\n\n", sep = "")
    obj <- obj_list[[nm]]
    if (inherits(obj, "ggplot")) {
      print(obj)
    } else if (is.data.frame(obj)) {
      cat(knitr::kable(obj, format = "pipe"), sep = "\n")
    }
    cat("\n\n")
  }
  cat(":::\n\n")
}



parse_slingshot()
The function parse_slingshot() parses the results out of the SingleCellExperiment object with the results. It returns all results needed for plots as tidy dataframes, so I can directly put the output into my visualization functions.
You provide the reduction you’ll need for visualization. By default it uses the reduction defined in the chunk define variables (which, in my case, is "HARMONY")
The argument vars_ridges selects the columns which can be used to create ridge plots. I defined these at the top in Defining variables, but use “condition” as default

parse_slingshot <- function(sce, reduction_plot = reduction, 
                            vars_ridges = "condition") {
  ## Pseudotime for DimReduc plot ----------------------------------------------
  
 pseudotime_dim <- slingPseudotime(sce)|>
   as_tibble(rownames = "barcode")
  
  # Extract dimensionality reduction embeddings
  dimred_coord <- reducedDim(sce, reduction_plot)[, 1:2] |> 
    as_tibble(rownames = "barcode")
  # Convert colnames of dimensionality reduction to dim1 and dim2, so I can
  # use these as variables in ggplot independently of what dimensionality
  # reduction needs to be plotted
  colnames(dimred_coord) <- c("barcode", "dim1", "dim2")
  
  # Join dimensionality reduction coordinates to pseudotime for DimReduc
  pseudotime_dim <- pseudotime_dim |>
    inner_join(dimred_coord, by = join_by(barcode))
  
  # Pivot_longer by lineage
  pseudotime_dim <- pseudotime_dim |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("Lineage"), 
      names_to = "Lineage",
      values_to = "pseudotime"
      )
  
  ## Average pseudotime for DimReduc plot --------------------------------------
  
  pseudotime_dim_avg <- slingAvgPseudotime(sce) |>
   as_tibble(rownames = "barcode") |> 
    dplyr::rename(pseudotime = value) |> # Sometimes uses S4package::rename
    inner_join(dimred_coord, by = join_by(barcode))
  
  ## Metadata for ridgeplots ---------------------------------------------------
  
  # Slingshot makes the pseudotime of each lineage a column in the metadata,
  # so I can simply extract the metadata. However, slingshot also stores a 
  # Slingshot object in the metadata, which is an S4 object. I need to remove 
  # this column to be able to use it as a tibble/df for ggplot
  metadata <- colData(sce)
  metadata <- metadata[, -which(names(metadata) == "slingshot")] |>
    as_tibble() |>
    select(
      starts_with("slingPseudotime"), # selects pseudotime column of all lineages
      "barcode", # needed for join with dimensionality reduction
      all_of(vars_ridges)
      ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("slingPseudotime"), 
      names_to = "Lineage",
      names_pattern = "(\\d+)", # Only keep the digit of the lineage
      values_to = "pseudotime"
      )
  
  ## Coordinates curves --------------------------------------------------------                          
  if (reduction_plot == reduction) {
    curves <- slingCurves(sce, as.df = TRUE)
  } else if (reduction_plot %in% reducedDimNames(sce)){
    embedded_curves <- embedCurves(sce, reduction_plot)
    curves <- slingCurves(embedded_curves, as.df = TRUE)
  } else {
    stop("You did not provide a dimensionality reduction which is in the sce")
  }
  # Rename the first two rows dim1 and dim2, so they're the same as in the
  # pseudotime_dim tibble
  names(curves)[1] <- "dim1"
  names(curves)[2] <- "dim2"
  # In pseudotime_dim, lineages are written as "Lineage1", whereas in curves,
  # lineages are written as "1". Make them the same for later ggplot use
  curves <- curves |>
    mutate(Lineage = paste0("Lineage", Lineage))
  
  # Bundle tibbles in list -----------------------------------------------------
  
  pseudotime_list <- list(
    "pseudotime_dim" = pseudotime_dim,
    "pseudotime_dim_avg" = pseudotime_dim_avg,
    "metadata" = metadata,
    "curves" = curves
  )
  pseudotime_list
}



plot_pseudotime()
plot_pseudotime() creates a scatterplot with the color indicating pseudotime and an overlaying line of the trajectory. I provided the option to either display individual lineages (as a facetted plot) or to display the average across lineages.
For the line of a lineage, I added two geom_paths: one black and one white. That makes a black line with a white border around it, which makes it easier to see, I think. I also applied ggrastr::geom_point_rast, as that makes the pdf size of manuscript figures managable.

plot_pseudotime <- function(
    pseudotime_list, 
    pseudotime_avg = FALSE, 
    pt_size = 0.3
    ) {
  pseudotime_dim_avg <- pseudotime_list$pseudotime_dim_avg
  pseudotime_dim <- pseudotime_list$pseudotime_dim
  curves <- pseudotime_list$curves
  
  if (pseudotime_avg) {
    p_pseudo <- ggplot(pseudotime_dim_avg, aes(x = dim1, y = dim2)) +
      ggrastr::geom_point_rast(aes(color = pseudotime), size = pt_size)  +
      scale_colour_viridis_c(na.value = "grey") +
      geom_path(
        data = curves  |> arrange(Order),
        mapping = aes(x = dim1, y = dim2, group = Lineage),
        linewidth = 1.75, color = "white"
      ) +
      geom_path(
        curves  |> arrange(Order), 
        mapping = aes(x = dim1, y = dim2, group = Lineage), 
        linewidth = 1.25,
        colour = "black"
        )
    p_pseudo <- p_pseudo + theme_classic()
  } else {
    p_pseudo <- ggplot() +
      ggrastr::geom_point_rast(
        data = pseudotime_dim,
        aes(x = dim1, y = dim2, color = pseudotime),
        size = pt_size
        ) +
      scale_colour_viridis_c(na.value = "grey") +
      geom_path(
        data = curves |> arrange(Order), 
        mapping = aes(x = dim1, y = dim2), 
        linewidth = 1.75,
        color = "white"
        ) +
      geom_path(

text:
Standard Seurat processing (Normalize, Variable Features, PCA, UMAP, etc.)
I wanted to remove sex chromosome genes and mitochondrial genes in the FindVariableFeatures step and created the helper function variable_feature_selection() to do so. The vector sexgenes should be specific for the genes which are and which are not in your Seurat object, so when I wanted to do this, Charlotte shared a text file with me. In hindsight, this was not the most reproducible or neat approach, but it is what I did all those months ago, so I’ll use it now as well. For transparancy, this sex_gene.txt file is also in the Git repo under /data/metainformation/sex_genes.txt.

seu <- NormalizeData(seu)

## Variable features -----------------------------------------------------------

# sex_genes.txt stores a list of sex genes in my seurat object 
file_txt <- file.path(dir_data_meta, "sex_genes.txt")
sexgenes <- read_table(file_txt, col_names = FALSE) |> pull(X1)

seu <- variable_feature_selection(seu, sexgenes)

## Further processing ----------------------------------------------------------

seu <- ScaleData(seu, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt")
seu <- RunPCA(seu) # Runs on variable features by default
seu <- RunHarmony(seu, group.by.vars = "AnonymousID")

Initializing centroids

# Seurat::RunUMAP sets a seed (seed.use = 42) by default, no need to do manually
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:dims)
seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, reduction = "harmony", k.param = k, dims = 1:dims)


## Join layers again -----------------------------------------------------------


# [name] seperated layers per participant for preprocessing (especially
# normalization). Later steps needs joined layers, so join them together again.
seu <- JoinLayers(seu)

title: 2. Discrete clustering
text:
Clustering itself: Seurat’s FindClusters()
Below, you can examine tabsets of our astrocytes clustered over multiple resolutions. I assessed multiple clustering resolutions and chose to continue with cluster resolution 0.15, as the three clusters created with resolution 0.15 remain robust over increasing resolutions (nicely illustrated in Figure 3). Higher resolutions create clusters which are hardly distinguishable from one another and which flow into one other (the borders become a bit blurry). You could run this script again with a different resolution in the section Defining variabless, but subsequent sections regarding cluster annotation assume cluster resolution 0.15, so it might be a little buggy if one changes resolution.

resolutions <- c(
  0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4,
  0.45, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0
)

plots_clust_pca <- list()
plots_clust_umap <- list()
for (resolution in resolutions) {
  seu <- FindClusters(
    seu,
    resolution = resolution,
    cluster.name = paste0("seurat_cluster_res", resolution),
    algorithm = 4 # 4 = Leiden algorithm
    )
  title <- paste0("Resolution ", resolution)
  p_clust_pca <- DimPlot(
    seu, 
    reduction = "pca", 
    group.by = paste0("seurat_cluster_res", resolution),
    raster = TRUE,
    pt.size = 2,
    label = TRUE
  ) +
    theme_manuscript() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")) +
    labs(title = title)
  p_clust_umap <- DimPlot(
    seu, 
    reduction = "umap", 
    group.by = paste0("seurat_cluster_res", resolution),
    raster = TRUE,
    pt.size = 2,
    label = TRUE
  )  +
    theme_manuscript() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")) +
    labs(title = title)
  # Can only save resolution as a string
  list_entry_name <- paste0("res", resolution)
  plots_clust_pca[[list_entry_name]] <- p_clust_pca
  plots_clust_umap[[list_entry_name]] <- p_clust_umap

Cluster interpretation and annotation

Removal cluster 4
I removed cluster 4, because the markers of that cluster mostly were mitochondrial RNA. I found that that was the case through Seurat’s FindAllMarkers().

Seurat’s FindAllMarkers()
I used Seurat’s function FindAllMarkers() to interpret clusters. By default, FindMarkers() sets threshold for the minimum log-Fold Chance threshold (logfc.threshold) and minumum percentage of cells expressing the gene (min.pct). I am generally in favour of setting these thresholds, but I will later use the output for Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), which also requires values for lowly expressed genes. Therefore, I run FindAllMarkers() with loose thresholds (logfc.threshold = 0 and min.pct = 0.1). Results of top markers are displayed below, using the function top_markers() which I defined above. I also saved a csv with the full results on disk, so I could inspect the full list myself.

# Run FindAllMarkers, but with very loose thresholds: I'll run GSEA of GO-terms
# on it, which means I'll want a gene score of almost all genes
markers <- FindAllMarkers(
  seu,
  logfc.threshold = 0,
  min.pct = 0.1
)

## Extract a table of top markers and save full table to disk
# I put top markers per cluster in a list to later display it as a tabset
list_markers <- list()
# Extract the number of clusters present in each resolution
marker_levels <- markers |>
  distinct(cluster) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.numeric(as.character(cluster)))
# The previous step created a dataframe, so select the column 'cluster'
for (i in marker_levels$cluster) {
  # Extract table of top markers and store in list
  list_entry_name <- paste0("Cluster ", i)
  list_markers[[list_entry_name]] <- top_markers(markers, cluster_select = i)
  # Write to disk as csv
  file_csv <- paste0("markers_", res, "_cluster", i, ".csv")
  file_csv <- file.path(dir_tab, file_csv)
  markers |>
    filter(cluster == i) |>
    write_csv(file_csv, col_names = TRUE, quote = "none")
}

Another distinction I could quickly make was a division in grey matter and white matter astrocytes. This dataset was annotated using reference atlases, and the atlas from the Allen Brain institue provided a white matter-grey matter astrocyte distinction. I came to the same conclusion using GO-terms. To test enrichment of pathways, I loaded in GO terms with the msigdbr package and used GO:Biological Processes (GO:BP). Some caveats:

The Seurat object contacts both genes given with SYMBOL and with EnsebmlID. SYMBOL genes are the standard, the EnsembleID genes in our data are either lnc-RNAs, transcript isoforms or other things - which are not in the GO:BP anyways. These are thus removed from the analysis.
For GSEA of GO terms, I need to sort genes, which can be done using either logFC or p-value. I designed my function to allow for both - either directly logFC or sign(logFC)*log(p). I mainly focused on direct logFC, mostly based on this GitHub discussion and the sources referenced there, but I acknowledge both methods have their limitations.


# Load in the gene set using msigdbr::msigdbr()
gs_go_bp <- msigdbr(
  species = "Homo sapiens", 
  collection = "C5", 
  subcollection = "GO:BP"
)
# Adapt the gene set to the input required for fgsea: it needs to be a list 
# with your pathways/gene set names and the genes that make up each pathway.
gene_sets <- split(x = gs_go_bp$gene_symbol, f = gs_go_bp$gs_name)

# Run GSEA for all clusters. For each cluster: save the output-table on disk and
# create a visualization. Use a list to store all visualizations.
# I would manually set clusters with marker_levels$cluster, so it works
# automatically, but that would include cluster 4, still, so I'll set it
# with 1:3
plot_list <- list()
for (i in 1:3) {
  gene_scores <- prepare_gsea(
    markers, 
    findallmarkers = TRUE, 
    identity = i, 
    sort = "logfc"
    )

  # Run GSEA with the fgsea package
  gsea_res <- fgsea(
    pathways = gene_sets, # List of gene sets to check
    stats = gene_scores,
    scoreType = 'std', # std as we have both pos and neg rankings
    minSize = 10, # otherwise I only get pathways with 2-5 genes
    maxSize = 500,
  )
  
  file_csv <- file.path(dir_tab, paste0("goterms_", res, "_cluster", i, ".csv"))
  write_csv(gsea_res, file_csv, col_names = TRUE, quote = "none")
  
  ## Create a visualization
  top_pathways <- gsea_pathway_selection(
    gsea_res, 
    n_up = number_of_top_pathways_up,
    n_down = number_of_top_pathways_down
    )
  
  p_gsea <- plotGseaTable(
    gene_sets[top_pathways], 
    stats = gene_scores, 
    fgseaRes = gsea_res, 
    headerLabelStyle = list(size = 14),
    pathwayLabelStyle = list(size = 12),
    valueStyle = list(size = 10),
    gseaParam = 0.5 # Makes the figure clearer
    )
  # Store the plot in the list under the name of the cluster
  list_entry_name <- paste0("Cluster ", i)
  plot_list[[list_entry_name]] <- p_gsea
}

Defining variables
This code block defines variables to be used throughout the rest of the document. If someone ever wants to run these scripts with different variables, they can easily change it here. I’ll substantiate any choices here

k
I tested Milo for multiple values of k (the K used for KNN graph building), but it had little effect on results. I therefore ended up using the default k value, which is 10.

title: 6. Differential abundance with Milo
6. Differential abundance with Milo
text:
Convert Seurat to Milo object
Milo requires its own type of object, the “Milo object”. To do so, I first had to convert my Seurat object to an sce object, after which I could turn the sce object into a milo object.

file_rds <- file.path(dir_data, "seu_shortread_astros_clustered.rds")
seu <- readRDS(file_rds)

## Seurat needs to be converted to sce
# Convert to an sce object
sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(seu)
# Milo requires a specific milo-object. The major differences between the Milo
# and SingleCellExperiment object are in the extra slots of the Milo object,
# such as those where nhood values are stored.
milo <- Milo(sce)

# Store the previously computed PCA and UMAP to the milo object
# For the PCA, use the integrated reduction ("harmony")
reducedDim(milo, "PCA") <- Embeddings(seu, reduction = "harmony")
reducedDim(milo, "UMAP") <- Embeddings(seu, reduction = "umap")

# Remove the Seurat and SCE objects to save memory
rm(seu)
rm(sce)

title: 6. Differential abundance with Milo
text:
Run Milo
I used all default settings to run Milo. One can change the k parameter in defining variables, I deliberately set this at 10.

# Construct a KNN graph. As I transfered the reduction "harmony" to the
# reductionname "PCA", it will automatically use this reduction for all
# following steps.
milo <- buildGraph(
  milo,
  k = k,
  d = 50, # default setting
)
# Define neighbourhoods. Settings are default
# This uses stochasticity, so set a seed
set.seed(42)
milo <- makeNhoods(
  milo,
  prop = 0.1,
  k = k,
  d = 50, # default setting
  refined = TRUE,
)

If the number of cells per neighborhood is too low, I should adapt the k parameter (tutorial recommends to have the distribution peaking above 20). It works well with my set k.

p_nhoodsize <- plotNhoodSizeHist(milo)
p_nhoodsize







Figure 1: The number of cells which belong to each neighborhood





The rest of milo works by analysing the cell counts per neighborhood per sample. In my data, the sample is given with the column “AnonymousID”.

milo <- countCells(
  milo,
  meta.data = data.frame(colData(milo)),
  sample = "AnonymousID"
)

To perform differential abundance testing with Milo, I need an additional dataframe with metadata. In my case, I want to test for the column “condition” (= ALS vs Ctrls). I first ran Milo months ago and my dplyr skills were not yet that good back then, so I got the solution below from here. Might as well still use it, but credit where credit’s due.

milo_design <- colData(milo) |>
  data.frame() |>
  select(AnonymousID, condition) |>
  distinct() |>
  remove_rownames() |>
  column_to_rownames("AnonymousID")
# Reorder rownames to match columns of nhoodCounts()
order_rows <- colnames(nhoodCounts(milo))
milo_design <- milo_design[order_rows, , drop = FALSE]


milo <- calcNhoodDistance(milo, d = 50) # Same d as buildGraph()

da_results <- testNhoods(
  milo,
  design = ~condition,
  design.df = milo_design
)


Inspect results

p_pval <- ggplot(da_results, aes(PValue)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50)
p_pval







Figure 2





You can already see that the results are skewed - I have way more ALS-depleted neighborhoods than ALS-enriched neighborhoods. This likely stems from the fact that we have just 4 controls, but 20 ALS samples.

p_logfc <- ggplot(da_results, aes(logFC, -log10(SpatialFDR))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1)
p_logfc







Figure 3





Add metadata to results by annotating neighborhoods by condition

# Annotate neighborhoods by condition
da_results <- annotateNhoods(milo, da_results, coldata_col = "condition")
# Categorize neighborhoods with < 70% of one condition as mixed
da_results$anno_condition <- ifelse(
  da_results$condition_fraction < 0.7,
  "Mixed",
  da_results$condition # The neighborhoods which are not mixed get ALS or Ctrl
)

Find group structure of neighborhoods. In practice, it runs louvain clustering to identify neighborhoods which are overlapping and thus similar to each other. The max.lfc.delta argument determines the cutoff of fold change, and can kind-of be considered like the resolution of a clustering algorithm. With one, I set it quite low.
The neighborhood graph is needed to map the results to an embedding. Each node will represent a neighbourhood and each edge indicates the number of cells the neighbourhouds have in common.

# Find group structure of neighborhoods
da_results <- groupNhoods(milo, da_results, max.lfc.delta = 1)

# Build a graph across the neighborhood groups
milo <- buildNhoodGraph(milo)

plotNhoodGraphDA directly visualizes the da_results, whereas plotNhoodGroups plots the groups created with groupNhoods. The alpha is the FDR significance threshold (0.05 is default). You can see that there are no clear ALS-enriched or -depleted populations.

p_nhood_da <- plotNhoodGraphDA(milo, da_results)
p_nhood_da







Figure 4






p_nhood_groups <- plotNhoodGroups(milo, da_results) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_nhood_groups







Figure 5






p_nhood_da + p_nhood_groups







Figure 6





Also test one where I do not set a significant threshold at all. Even then, you do not see clear ALS-enriched or -depleted populations.

p_nhood_da_loose <- plotNhoodGraphDA(milo, da_results, alpha = 1)
p_nhood_da_loose







Figure 7

title: 8. Creating the astrocyte-junction Seurat
text:
The nuclei in this project were sequenced twice: half of each barcoded library with short-read and half with long-read sequencing. Scripts 01-07 analysed the short-read data. This script (together with 09 and 10) uses the long-read data to look at exon junctions: places where a read goes from one exon to the next on the reference genome, where each junction is stored as a string chr:start:end. We created a junction count matrix, in which each each column is a nucleus and each row is a junction, which can easily be turned into a Seurat object (a regular Seurat object has the genes as rows, instead of junctions). Because the nuclei are the same as in the short-read data, I can transfer the short-read annotation and dimensionality reductions to the junction data.
The script has two parts:

Junction matrix and QC. I load the junction count matrix, filter junctions, compute per-nucleus QC metrics (including the fraction of reads from known / novel junctions), filter nuclei and store the result as a Seurat object. The code of this part was originally written by [name]; I rewrote it to understand how it works.
Astrocyte selection and gene-specific preprocessing. I select the astrocytes (the barcodes of the short-read astrocyte object), transfer the cluster annotation, PCA and UMAP, filter junctions again within astrocytes and then create one Seurat object per gene of interest. These are normalised with TF-IDF (junction matrices are even sparser than gene expression matrices) and stored for scripts 09 (differential expression between clusters) and 10 (pseudobulk differential expression, ALS vs control).

Disclaimer: the code within part 1 this script was actually not written by me: I recieved an Rscript with this code from Tom van Schaik. I did convert all steps to a Quarto format and feel like I fully understand what is happening, but I do not claim credit for this code.

}

  mutate(

      str_detect(AnonymousID, "Ctrl") == TRUE,

# (I group by AnonymousID, so it should be fine)
stopifnot(group_var %in% colnames(seu@meta.data))



Junction annotation status
junction_features.tsv.gz contains information per junction, including whether the junction (or its donor / acceptor site) is already annotated (annotation_status) and whether it is canonical. I use this to calculate, per nucleus, which percentage of its reads comes from known, partially known, novel and canonical junctions. junc_meta is also used in part 2 of this script, to find the junctions of a gene.

stopifnot(file.exists(file_junc_feat))

cat("Loading junction features from:", file_junc_feat, "\n")

Loading junction features from: /path/to/folder/projects/snrna_astros_shortread_postQC/data/raw/longread/junction_features.tsv.gz 

junc_meta <- read.table(
  file_junc_feat, header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE
)
if ("canonical" %in% colnames(junc_meta)) {
  junc_meta$canonical <- as.logical(junc_meta$canonical) # was <chr>
}
rownames(junc_meta) <- junc_meta$junction_id

# Only keep junctions which are in the Seurat object
junc_meta <- junc_meta[intersect(rownames(seu), rownames(junc_meta)), , drop = FALSE]
cat("  ", nrow(junc_meta), " / ", nrow(seu), " junctions in annotation table\n", sep = "")

  513293 / 513692 junctions in annotation table



cat("Computing per-cell annotation fractions...\n")

Computing per-cell annotation fractions...

mat <- GetAssayData(seu, layer = "counts")
total_reads <- Matrix::colSums(mat)

for (status in annotation_statuses) {
  # Junction IDs with this annotation status
  jids <- rownames(junc_meta)[
    !is.na(junc_meta$annotation_status) & junc_meta$annotation_status == status
  ]
  jids <- intersect(jids, rownames(mat))
  status_reads <- if (length(jids) > 0) {
    Matrix::colSums(mat[jids, , drop = FALSE])
  } else {
    rep(0, ncol(mat))
  }

}

# Same for canonical junctions
canonical_jids <- rownames(junc_meta)[
  !is.na(junc_meta$canonical) & junc_meta$canonical
]
canonical_jids <- intersect(canonical_jids, rownames(mat))
canonical_reads <- if (length(canonical_jids) > 0) {
  Matrix::colSums(mat[canonical_jids, , drop = FALSE])
} else {
  rep(0, ncol(mat))
}
seu[["pct_canonical"]] <- canonical_reads / total_reads * 100

pct_cols <- c(paste0("pct_", annotation_statuses), "pct_canonical")
for (col in pct_cols) {

}

title: 8. Creating the astrocyte-junction Seurat
text:
Gene-specific Seurat objects
A lot happens in this loop, so let me write it out. For each gene in genes, this loop:

selects the junctions of this gene using junc_meta and stores the junction information as a .csv;
subsets the astrocyte Seurat to these junctions;
removes nuclei without any reads for this gene. Because of the low read depth of long-read sequencing, many nuclei do not express any junction of a specific gene. Keeping them would cause a mathematical error in the normalisation (division by zero);
normalises the data (TF-IDF by default [source]);
saves the object as data/processed/junction_seurat_<gene>.rds.

For TF-IDF normalisation I do the following:

IDF: the log of total nuclei divided by the number of nuclei in which a junction is detected. A junction detected in most nuclei gets a low number, a junction detected in only a few nuclei gets a high number.
TF: the raw matrix is multiplied by a diagonal matrix which divides every value in a column by the column total (%*% is matrix multiplication). In effect: what fraction of this nucleus’ junction reads comes from each junction?
TF-IDF: every junction’s TF row is multiplied by its IDF. The scale factor is applied before the log to keep values out of the log’s dead zone, just like Seurat’s LogNormalize() does.


gene_summary <- list()

for (gene in genes) {
  cat("## For loop on gene:", gene, "\n")
  
  # Junction information of this gene. Some entries in the gene_name column
  # have the format "ENSEMBLID, SYMBOL", so I use str_detect() instead of ==
  gene_junctions_df <- junc_meta |>
    dplyr::filter(str_detect(gene_name, gene))
  
  # Store the meta-information of the junctions of this gene, so I can still
  # inspect it later if I want to
  file_csv <- file.path(dir_tab, paste0("junction_meta_", gene, ".csv"))
  write_csv(gene_junctions_df, file_csv)
  
  # Junctions of this gene which survived the filtering steps
  gene_junctions <- intersect(
    gene_junctions_df$junction_id, 
    rownames(seu_junctions_astro)
  )
  cat("  ", nrow(gene_junctions_df), " annotated junctions, ",
      length(gene_junctions), " left after filtering\n", sep = "")
  if (length(gene_junctions) == 0) {
    cat("  No junctions left for", gene, "- skipping this gene\n")
    next
  }
  
  seu_gene <- subset(seu_junctions_astro, features = gene_junctions)
  
  ## Remove empty cells for this specific gene ---------------------------------
  
  cat("Filtering out empty cells for", gene, "\n")
  n_cells_total <- ncol(seu_gene)
  
  # Boolean column: does this nucleus have reads for any junction of this gene?
  mat_raw <- GetAssayData(seu_gene, layer = "counts")
  seu_gene$has_gene <- Matrix::colSums(mat_raw) >= min_cell_gene
  
  cat("The number of cells with junctions for this gene is:\n")
  print(table(seu_gene$has_gene))
  cat("And per cluster:\n")
  print(table(
    has_gene = seu_gene$has_gene, 
    annotation = seu_gene@meta.data[[annotation_var]]
  ))
  
  if (sum(seu_gene$has_gene) == 0) {
    cat("  No cells express", gene, "- skipping this gene\n")
    next
  }
  
  seu_gene <- subset(seu_gene, subset = has_gene) # has_gene is a Boolean
  
  ## Normalisation -------------------------------------------------------------
  
  # IMPORTANT: extract the counts AFTER removing the empty cells. In the R
  # script, mat_raw was extracted before the removal. The empty cells then
  # had a column total of 0 (1 / 0 = Inf in the TF step) and the dimensions
  # of the TF-IDF matrix did not match those of the Seurat object.
  mat_raw <- GetAssayData(seu_gene, layer = "counts")
  
  if (norm_method == "tfidf") {
    cat("Normalising (TF-IDF, scale.factor =", tfidf_scale_factor, ")\n")
    
    idf <- log(1 + ncol(mat_raw) / Matrix::rowSums(mat_raw > 0))
    tf <- mat_raw %*% Matrix::Diagonal(x = 1 / Matrix::colSums(mat_raw))
    tfidf <- log1p(Matrix::Diagonal(x = idf * tfidf_scale_factor) %*% tf)
    
    # Matrix multiplication with a Diagonal() matrix can lose the dimnames
    dimnames(tfidf) <- dimnames(mat_raw)
    
    # Sanity checks before putting it in the Seurat object
    stopifnot(
      identical(dim(tfidf), dim(mat_raw)),
      identical(rownames(tfidf), rownames(seu_gene)),
      identical(colnames(tfidf), colnames(seu_gene)),
      all(is.finite(tfidf@x))
    )
    
    # Set the normalised matrix as 'data', as this is also where
    # LogNormalize() stores the normalised data.
    seu_gene <- SetAssayData(seu_gene, layer = "data", new.data = tfidf)
    
    rm(idf, tf, tfidf)
  } else if (norm_method == "lognorm") {
    seu_gene <- NormalizeData(seu_gene, verbose = FALSE)
  } else {
    stop("You did not provide an available normalization method. Choose 'tfidf' or 'lognorm'")
  }
  
  # Store the normalisation method in the object, so 09 and 10 can report it
  seu_gene@misc$normalization <- norm_method
  
  ## Save to disk --------------------------------------------------------------
  
  file_rds_gene <- file.path(dir_data, paste0("junction_seurat_", gene, ".rds"))
  cat("Saving Seurat object to:", file_rds_gene, "\n")
  saveRDS(seu_gene, file_rds_gene)
  cat("Seurat saved!\n")
  
  gene_summary[[gene]] <- tibble(
    gene = gene,
    n_junctions = nrow(seu_gene),
    n_cells_before_filter = n_cells_total,
    n_cells_with_gene = ncol(seu_gene),
    normalisation = norm_method
  )
  
  rm(seu_gene, mat_raw); gc()
}

title: 10. Junction differential expression; ALS vs control (pseudobulk)
text:
In script 08 I created gene-specific junction Seurat objects of the astrocytes (normalised with TF-IDF). In this script I test which junctions of a gene differ between ALS patients and controls. Instead of treating every nucleus as an independent observation, I create a pseudobulk per donor: the raw junction counts of all astrocytes of a donor are summed, and the resulting donor-by-junction count matrix is tested with DESeq2 (design ~ condition, with Ctrl as reference level). Script 09 tests differential expression between clusters instead.
For every gene, the DESeq2 results are stored as a .csv (sorted by raw p-value). The results are visualised with an MA plot, a dotplot of the top junctions and violin plots per junction (counts and normalised data). The helper functions also contain the functions to draw an exon junction relative to a reference transcript, which I can use on the junctions I find interesting.
